questions.title: How exactly does OFT preserve pairwise angles between neurons when left-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: The paper says OFT preserves the pairwise angles between neurons by transforming all neurons in a layer with the same orthogonal matrix. If a pretrained linear layer has weight matrix $\mathbf{W}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ and OFT uses $\mathbf{R} \in O(d)$ so the finetuned weights are $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0$, then each neuron (column) changes from $\mathbf{w}_i^0$ to $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_i^0$. I know orthogonal matrices preserve inner products in $\mathbb{R}^d$, but here the columns live in the $d$-dimensional input space while the outputs are $n$-dimensional. Could someone confirm formally that for any pair of columns $\mathbf{w}_i^0, \mathbf{w}_j^0$, the angle between $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_i^0$ and $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}_j^0$ equals that between $\mathbf{w}_i^0$ and $\mathbf{w}_j^0$? Is this still true when $n \neq d$?

questions.title: Why is the Cayley transform always safe (invertible) for parameterizing orthogonal matrices in OFT/BOFT?
questions.question_body: Both OFT and BOFT use the Cayley parameterization $\mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{Q} = -\mathbf{Q}^\top$. I understand $\mathbf{Q}$ is skew-symmetric, but I'm concerned about the invertibility of $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})$. Is there a simple argument that $\det(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}) \neq 0$ for all real skew-symmetric $\mathbf{Q}$, so that the Cayley transform cannot blow up during training? Does this hold in finite precision, and are there any practical regularization tricks to avoid numerical issues?

questions.title: What exactly are “free edges” in the information transmission view, and how do they map to trainable parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a grid-graph view where composing $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{B}_m\cdots\mathbf{B}_1$ corresponds to information flow across levels, and mentions desiderata like dense connectivity and minimum free edges. It also says some edges are "not trainable" (e.g., the $d$ edges required for bijection between adjacent levels in an orthogonal matrix) and should not be counted. Can you provide a precise definition of which edges correspond to fixed structure (e.g., permutations or $\pm 1$ entries) versus edges that introduce free parameters? How does this edge counting reproduce the parameter counts for block-diagonal OFT and for BOFT?

questions.title: Derivation of the parameter count: why does BOFT($m,b$) have \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) effective trainable parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BOFT($m,b$) has $\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm$ effective trainable parameters for a $d\times n$ linear layer. I’m trying to reconcile this with the fact that each butterfly component can be permuted into block-diagonal $2b\times 2b$ orthogonal blocks, each of which (if unconstrained) would have $\tfrac{(2b)(2b-1)}{2}$ degrees of freedom. Could you walk through the step-by-step counting that accounts for the butterfly sparsity/permutation so that the total reduces to $\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm$? Which constraints eliminate the other degrees of freedom?

questions.title: How does BOFT achieve a dense orthogonal matrix with \(\mathcal{O}(d\log d)\) parameters when \(m=\log d, b=2\)?
questions.question_body: For $m = \log d$ and $b=2$, the paper claims that BOFT uses $\mathcal{O}(d\log d)$ parameters yet yields a dense orthogonal $\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$. Could you show explicitly how the product of $m$ sparse orthogonal butterfly components (each with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ nonzeros) creates a dense matrix? Is there an intuitive argument, via the information transmission graph, that every input coordinate reaches every output coordinate after $\log d$ stages?

questions.title: Is BOFT equivalent to a constrained composition of Givens rotations?
questions.question_body: Classically, any orthogonal matrix can be decomposed into a product of $2\times 2$ Givens rotations, which also preserves orthogonality. BOFT’s orthogonal butterfly components look like structured compositions of many $2\times 2$ orthogonals (or $2b\times 2b$ blocks). Is BOFT essentially restricting the sequence and pairing pattern of these Givens-like rotations to follow the butterfly topology? If so, how does this restriction compare in expressivity and parameter-efficiency to a generic sequence of Givens rotations?

questions.title: What happens when \(d\) is not a power of two? How to construct butterfly components and ensure orthogonality?
questions.question_body: The definitions of butterfly factors and components assume $d=2^N$ and $k$ a power of 2. In practice, linear layers often have arbitrary input dimensions $d$. How does BOFT handle non-power-of-two $d$? Do you pad to the next power of two and then mask out extra dimensions, or is there a more parameter-efficient generalization? How does this affect the orthogonality and parameter counts?

questions.title: Does multiplicative dropout preserve orthogonality and does it bias the gradient estimator?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a multiplicative Dropout that replaces randomly selected $2b\times 2b$ blocks inside butterfly components with identity matrices during training. Since identity is orthogonal, the resulting product remains orthogonal at each forward pass. But does this stochastic replacement introduce bias in the gradient of the expected loss with respect to the original continuous parameters? Is there any analysis on whether this acts like a regularizer versus simply reducing capacity during training-time only? Also, is there a recommended schedule for $(p_1, p_2)$ to avoid underfitting?

questions.title: How does BOFT offer a “smoother interpolation” between full expressivity and identity compared to block-diagonal OFT?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BOFT provides a smoother interpolation between the full orthogonal group (expressivity) and the identity matrix (regularity) than OFT’s block-diagonal structure. Can you formalize this notion of "smoother interpolation"? For example, is there a principled path or homotopy in parameter space controlled by $(m,b)$ such that increasing $m$ or decreasing $b$ increases expressivity monotonically? How does this compare to simply enlarging block sizes in OFT?

questions.title: Runtime complexity: how do costs of BOFT compare with full OFT and block-diagonal OFT during training and inference?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions a slight runtime overhead for BOFT during training, but zero extra inference latency after folding $\mathbf{R}$ into $\mathbf{W}^0$. Could you quantify the per-forward/backward cost of applying $\mathbf{R}=\prod_{i=1}^m \tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b_{(d,i)}$? Naively, each component has $\mathcal{O}(d)$ nonzeros, so total should be $\mathcal{O}(md)$ per application versus $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ for a full dense orthogonal and $\mathcal{O}(bd)$ for block-diagonal OFT. Is this the right way to think about it, and how does it translate to wall-clock on GPUs?

questions.title: Clarifying the “dense connectivity” condition in the transmission view: is path existence sufficient?
questions.question_body: In the grid-graph formulation, a product $\mathbf{B}_m\cdots\mathbf{B}_1$ is said to be dense if every first-level node reaches every last-level node. Is mere existence of a directed path sufficient to guarantee that the corresponding entry in $\mathbf{R}$ can be non-zero, or are additional constraints (like orthogonality or path overlaps) needed for that entry to actually attain a non-zero value? Can there be topologies where paths exist but orthogonality constraints force some entries to zero?

questions.title: Why can’t block-diagonal OFT approximate classic linear transforms like FFT or DCT?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that the block-diagonal structure in OFT reduces expressiveness and "cannot approximate classic linear transforms." Is there a straightforward argument why a block-diagonal orthogonal cannot approximate transforms such as the DFT or DCT matrices? For instance, is it because those transforms mix all coordinates globally while any block-diagonal matrix only mixes coordinates within blocks, leaving strict zeros elsewhere?

questions.title: Interpreting BOFT as learning a bilinear similarity: what is the advantage of orthogonality vs. general PSD metrics?
questions.question_body: BOFT can be seen as learning a bilinear form $\mathbf{w}_i^{0\top}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{R}$ constrained to be orthogonal. In metric learning, one often learns a PSD matrix (e.g., $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{L}^\top\mathbf{L}$) to define a Mahalanobis distance or similarity. What are the benefits of restricting to $\mathbf{R} \in O(d)$ versus allowing a general PSD metric? Is the key advantage here the spectral norm preservation and stability, or are there other inductive biases at play?

questions.title: How does the spectral norm preservation help in practice, and is it exact with floating-point arithmetic?
questions.question_body: Orthogonal finetuning preserves the spectral norm of $\mathbf{W}^0$ because $\|\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\|_2 = \|\mathbf{W}^0\|_2$ for $\mathbf{R}\in O(d)$. In practice, with Cayley parameterization and floating-point arithmetic, is this preservation exact up to machine precision, or can it drift? Do you observe better training stability (e.g., fewer exploding activations/gradients) empirically attributable to this property compared to LoRA?

questions.title: Understanding Theorem 1: how do products of butterfly and transposed butterfly matrices span the full orthogonal group?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size and that a product of butterfly matrices and their transposes like $\mathbf{B}_{d-1,1}(d)\mathbf{B}^\top_{d-1,2}(d)\cdots\mathbf{B}_{1,1}(d)\mathbf{B}^\top_{1,2}(d)$ can approximate all orthogonal matrices for suitable depth. Could you sketch the proof or intuition? Is this connected to a factorization of arbitrary orthogonals into a kaleidoscope hierarchy similar to how Givens rotations generate $O(d)$?

questions.title: What is the precise meaning of “effective trainable parameters” under orthogonality constraints?
questions.question_body: The paper repeatedly refers to "effective trainable parameters" being less than the number of non-zero entries, because orthogonality introduces dependencies. How exactly do you define and count these effective parameters? Is it the manifold dimension of the parameterized subset of $O(d)$ (e.g., counting independent skew-symmetric entries after structure is imposed by the butterfly pattern), or something else tied to the specific Cayley blocks?

questions.title: How is BOFT applied to different module shapes in transformers (e.g., Q/K/V, output projections, MLPs)?
questions.question_body: In transformers, linear layers have shapes like $d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{model}}$, $d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{ff}}$, etc. The paper defines OFT/BOFT as left-multiplying $\mathbf{W}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ by $\mathbf{R}\in O(d)$. For non-square layers (e.g., $d\neq n$), is $d$ always the input dimension? When adapting LLMs or ViTs, do you apply a separate $\mathbf{R}$ to each linear map (Q, K, V, O, MLP up/down) with its own input dimension, or share $\mathbf{R}$ across certain groups? Any observed best practices?

questions.title: Initialization and training path: how does BOFT realize the claimed “weight interpolation” phenomenon?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an "intriguing weight interpolation" (Figure referenced) enabled by the matrix factorization. Is the idea that the product $\mathbf{R} = \prod_{i=1}^m \tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b_{(d,i)}$ provides a natural path from identity to the final transform by gradually turning on factors or scaling the skew-symmetric parameters (e.g., $\mathbf{Q} \mapsto t\mathbf{Q}$ within Cayley)? Could you describe concretely how to construct such an interpolation path and whether it has any empirical benefits (e.g., smoother loss landscapes)?

questions.title: How does BOFT compare to LoRA in terms of representational bias: sparse mixing vs. low-rank updates?
questions.question_body: LoRA adds a low-rank matrix $\Delta\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$ while BOFT multiplies by a structured orthogonal $\mathbf{R}$. Can you provide intuition or examples where sparse-composition orthogonals capture useful transformations that low-rank additive updates struggle with (or vice versa)? For a fixed parameter budget, are there tasks where low-rank is inherently better aligned than orthogonal mixing, or does BOFT’s stability give it a consistent edge?

questions.title: Empirical stability: do products of multiple Cayley-parameterized components accumulate numerical error?
questions.question_body: Although each $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b_{(d,i)}$ is orthogonal by construction, the product of many such matrices could still suffer from numerical drift in finite precision. Do you observe any loss of orthogonality (e.g., $\|\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\|_F$ growing) during long training runs? If so, do you re-orthogonalize periodically or rely on reparameterization at each forward pass to keep $\mathbf{R}$ on the manifold?
